acceptable.choice: Laravel for the app (API, agent dashboard, auth, billing, message storage) with Laravel Reverb as a separate WebSocket server process
acceptable.why: The founder already knows Laravel, so they ship fastest. Reverb is Laravel's own WebSocket server: it runs on an event loop, uses the Pusher protocol and works with Laravel broadcasting and Echo, so long-lived widget connections stay out of PHP-FPM.

acceptable.choice: Scale Reverb horizontally across a few VMs, using Redis pub/sub between the nodes and a WebSocket-aware load balancer or nginx proxy
acceptable.why: 2,000 connections fits on one small node. 50,000 is a few nodes behind Redis, which suits their plan of a few cloud VMs and keeps hosting cheap.

acceptable.choice: Soketi (self-hosted, Pusher-compatible) as an alternative WebSocket server behind Laravel broadcasting
acceptable.why: It speaks the same Pusher protocol, so Laravel and Echo code doesn't change. It's a fair fallback if Reverb falls short in load tests, but it is a Node service to run and is less actively maintained.

acceptable.choice: A managed Pusher-protocol service (Pusher Channels or Ably) during the first year
acceptable.why: No WebSocket infrastructure to run while they find product fit, and the Pusher protocol lets them switch to self-hosted Reverb later without changing app code. Pricing per connection gets expensive near 50,000, so it's a starting point, not the long-term answer.

acceptable.choice: Redis for queues (with Horizon), broadcasting and presence/ephemeral state, and Postgres or MySQL for messages
acceptable.why: This is the standard Laravel setup the founder already knows, and it is enough for this load.

acceptable.choice: A lightweight embeddable widget in vanilla JS, Preact or Svelte using laravel-echo/pusher-js, with typing indicators sent as client events (whispers)
acceptable.why: The widget runs on other companies' sites, so it must be small. Sending typing indicators as whispers keeps them off the database and the queue.

acceptable.choice: Laravel Octane (Swoole, RoadRunner or FrankenPHP) for the HTTP side if it's needed later
acceptable.why: It's an optional throughput improvement for API and auth endpoints. It doesn't solve WebSockets and isn't needed on day one.

ruled_out.choice: Rewriting from day one in Elixir/Phoenix, Go or Node.js because 'PHP can't do real-time'
ruled_out.why: Neither founder has these skills, so shipping slows. The concurrency goal is reachable from Laravel with an event-loop WebSocket server, so a rewrite buys nothing they need.

ruled_out.choice: Holding widget connections in PHP-FPM through long-polling or SSE
ruled_out.why: Every open connection occupies a whole FPM worker, so thousands of widgets would need thousands of PHP processes. That breaks concurrency first and hosting cost second.

ruled_out.choice: Short polling from the widget (for example every 1–3 seconds)
ruled_out.why: Messages aren't instant, and 50,000 widgets polling all the time creates huge request volume and cost.

ruled_out.choice: Livewire, or any server-rendered and stateful approach, for the embedded customer widget
ruled_out.why: The widget runs inside third-party pages and must be light, isolated and connection-efficient. Livewire is fine for the internal agent dashboard but not for the widget.

ruled_out.choice: Pusher or Ably as the permanent answer at 50,000 connections
ruled_out.why: Per-connection pricing at that scale conflicts with hosting cost, their second priority. It's fine early if they can move to Reverb later.

ruled_out.choice: Kubernetes, microservices or a custom-built WebSocket cluster from day one
ruled_out.why: Too much operational work for two founders. A few VMs running Laravel, Reverb, Redis and a database cover the three-year target.

ruled_out.choice: Firebase or Supabase Realtime as the core chat backend instead of Laravel
ruled_out.why: It throws away the founder's Laravel strength, splits the backend in two, and brings its own lock-in and per-usage costs.

must_mention: Yes, keep Laravel. The real decision is to keep long-lived connections out of PHP-FPM and run a dedicated event-loop WebSocket server (Reverb, or a Pusher-protocol equivalent) next to the Laravel app.
2,000 concurrent connections is small and one modest Reverb node handles it. 50,000 is reachable by scaling Reverb horizontally with Redis pub/sub across a few VMs.

Production Reverb needs OS and runtime tuning: a raised open-file limit (ulimit/nofile), and an event-loop extension such as ext-uv, because the default stream_select loop caps out at about 1,024 connections. The nginx or load balancer in front must support WebSocket upgrades and long idle timeouts.
Typing indicators and other ephemeral events should go as client-to-client whispers or through Redis, never through queued jobs and database writes. Only real messages get persisted.
Broadcasting from Laravel should go through a Redis queue worker (Horizon) so HTTP requests aren't slowed by fan-out.

Plan auth for anonymous widget visitors: per-visitor or per-conversation private channels, a cheap token-based channel auth endpoint, and keys scoped per customer so tenants can't read each other's conversations.
Use the Pusher protocol (Echo/pusher-js) so the WebSocket backend can be swapped between Reverb, Soketi and Pusher/Ably without rewriting the app.
Load-test the WebSocket layer before 50,000 is real, including reconnect storms after deploys or node restarts (clients should reconnect with jittered backoff).
red_flags: Telling them Laravel or PHP is the wrong choice and they must start in Elixir, Go or Node, ignoring their skills and their timeline.
Claiming PHP fundamentally can't hold many concurrent WebSocket connections, without mentioning Reverb, ReactPHP or Swoole.
Recommending long-polling or SSE served by PHP-FPM workers, or short polling, as the real-time transport.
Recommending Pusher or Ably for the whole three years without warning about cost at 50,000 connections.
Leaving out the ~1,024-connection stream_select limit and file-descriptor tuning, so the first deploy quietly caps out.
Routing typing indicators through the database or the job queue.
Proposing Kubernetes, microservices, Kafka or multi-region setups for a two-person pre-launch team.
Recommending Livewire or a heavy SPA framework for the third-party embedded widget.
Treating Laravel Octane as the WebSocket solution.
unknowns: Message and typing-event rates per connection, and broadcast fan-out (how many agents watch each conversation). This drives Reverb node count and Redis load more than the raw connection count does.
How many connections a single Reverb node handles on their chosen VM size. This needs a load test.
Whether agent dashboards and mobile apps add significantly to the connection count beyond customer widgets.
How much budget there is for a managed service in year one compared with the operational time it costs to self-host.
Data residency, retention and compliance needs of their customers (GDPR, region-specific hosting), which may constrain where VMs and managed services can sit.
Whether the 50,000 projection materializes and how spiky the traffic is (business hours, time zones).
Latency requirements across regions, which would decide whether one region is enough.
